title: Node.js, Express.js, and REST APIs
description: Master the Node.js runtime, build web servers with Express routing and middleware, and design secure, well-tested REST APIs with proper status codes, validation, and error handling.
objectives: Explain the Node.js event loop and write non-blocking asynchronous code
Structure Node.js applications with modules, npm, and package.json
Build Express servers with routing, middleware, and error handling
Design RESTful resources with correct methods, status codes, and idempotency
Validate input, secure endpoints, and test APIs with Supertest

modules.title: Node.js Runtime Essentials
modules.description: How Node runs JavaScript outside the browser: the event loop, modules, and asynchronous patterns.
modules.completionCriteria: Write a script that performs concurrent async work and handles failures without blocking the event loop.

lessons.title: The Event Loop and Non-Blocking I/O
objectives: Explain why Node is single-threaded yet concurrent
Predict execution order of timers and microtasks

content.introduction: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single thread but handles many connections at once by never waiting for slow work — it delegates I/O to the OS and continues running other code.
content.explanation: When you call an asynchronous API like fs.readFile, Node hands the operation to a libuv worker and returns immediately, registering a callback for later. Once the work finishes, the event loop places the callback in a queue and runs it when the main call stack is empty. This is why ordering surprises beginners: synchronous code always runs first, then microtasks (promises), then timers in registration order. Blocking the stack with a heavy loop freezes every pending callback, so long CPU work must be chunked or moved off the main thread.

examples.title: Execution order of sync, timer, and promise code
examples.walkthrough: The two sync logs run first, the promise microtask beats the zero-delay timer, and the timer runs last once the stack is empty.

content.useCase: Serving thousands of concurrent HTTP connections from a single process without a thread per request.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why can Node handle many concurrent connections with one thread?
options: It offloads I/O to the OS and runs callbacks later on the event loop
It spawns one thread per request
It runs JavaScript in parallel threads
It blocks until every request finishes
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Non-blocking I/O means the thread never waits; callbacks run when results arrive.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the output of the example?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Sync logs finish first, then promise microtasks, then timers.

content.summary: Node is single-threaded and non-blocking: I/O goes to the OS, callbacks run on the event loop, and microtasks precede timers.

lessons.title: Modules, npm, and package.json
objectives: Split code across files with CommonJS or ESM
Manage dependencies with npm and package.json

content.introduction: Node gives you a module system for splitting code and npm for sharing it — together they keep a codebase navigable and its dependencies explicit.
content.explanation: CommonJS uses require to load and module.exports to expose, and it resolves synchronously from the filesystem. ES modules use import/export, require "type": "module" in package.json (or an .mjs extension), and are parsed statically so imports are hoisted. package.json is the contract for your project: name, entry point, scripts, and dependencies. A dependency in "dependencies" ships to production; one in "devDependencies" (test runners, linters) is only needed at build time — putting a tool in the wrong bucket bloats your deployment.

examples.title: Exporting and consuming a module
examples.walkthrough: config.js exports a plain object; server.js requires it by relative path and exports its own function, keeping each file focused.

content.useCase: Any project larger than a single file: shared utilities, route handlers, and configuration split into modules.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where does a package used only for unit tests belong?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Test runners are build-time tools and should not ship to production.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which pair of keywords is used in CommonJS?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: CommonJS loads with require and exposes values via module.exports.

content.summary: Modules split code; npm manages dependencies. Keep runtime and dev dependencies in the right package.json bucket.

lessons.title: Promises, async/await, and Error Handling
objectives: Write async functions with try/catch
Run independent work concurrently with Promise.all

content.introduction: Promises represent a value that arrives later; async/await lets you write that asynchronous flow like straight-line code.
content.explanation: An async function always returns a promise, and await pauses that function (not the thread) until the promise settles. Rejections thrown inside async functions become rejected promises, so a plain try/catch around await works — but a catch that swallows the error hides failures; rethrow or log and translate it into a response. When operations are independent, start them all before awaiting so they run concurrently: awaiting sequentially turns what could be one round trip into several.

examples.title: Concurrent fetches with error handling
examples.walkthrough: Promise.all starts all three requests immediately and rejects if any fails; the original error is logged before a safe error is rethrown.

content.useCase: API gateways and dashboards that aggregate several backend calls into one response.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does await pause?
options: Only the current async function, not the event loop
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Other callbacks keep running while one function waits on a promise.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why start independent promises before awaiting them?
options: So they execute concurrently instead of one after another
So they run on separate threads
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Awaiting sequentially serializes work that could overlap.

content.summary: async/await makes asynchronous code readable. Start independent work first, and never swallow rejections.

modules.title: Express Routing & Middleware
modules.description: Map URLs to handlers and organize request processing as a chain of middleware.
modules.completionCriteria: Build an Express app with parameterized routes, a reusable middleware chain, and centralized error handling.

lessons.title: Routes, Params, and Route Handlers
objectives: Declare routes for HTTP methods
Read path, query, and body parameters

content.introduction: A route pairs an HTTP method and a URL pattern with a handler function that produces the response.
content.explanation: Express matches incoming requests in registration order: app.get("/jobs/:id", handler) fires only for GET requests whose path fits the pattern. Params come from the path (req.params.id), filters from the query string (req.query), and payloads from the body (req.body) — the body is only populated after express.json() parses it. Because matching is sequential, put specific routes like /jobs/featured before generic ones like /jobs/:id, or the parameterized route will swallow them.

examples.title: A parameterized route
examples.walkthrough: req.params.id reads the path segment, express.json() enables body parsing, and the POST handler answers 201 with a Location header.

content.useCase: Any CRUD API where each resource has a collection URL and a per-item URL.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where does req.params come from?
options: Dynamic segments of the URL path
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Placeholders like :id are extracted into req.params.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is express.json() needed before reading req.body?
options: It parses the JSON payload into a JavaScript object
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Without a body parser, req.body is undefined for JSON requests.

content.summary: Routes match method plus path. Read params from the path, query from the URL, and body only after parsing middleware.

lessons.title: The Middleware Pipeline
objectives: Explain the (req, res, next) contract
Write and mount reusable middleware

content.introduction: Middleware functions run in sequence between the request and the response — logging, auth, parsing, and finally your handler.
content.explanation: Each middleware receives req, res, and next, and must either end the response or call next() to pass control onward; forgetting next() stalls the request until it times out. Middleware can be mounted app-wide, per router, or on a single route, which lets you apply expensive checks only where they matter. This pipeline is where cross-cutting concerns live: one logger for every request, one auth check for protected routes, one CORS policy for the whole API.

examples.title: A request logger and a mounted router
examples.walkthrough: requestLogger passes control on and measures after the response finishes; requireApiKey stops unauthorized requests before the router runs.

content.useCase: Request logging, authentication, rate limiting, and CORS applied consistently across an API.

knowledgeCheck.question: What must a middleware do to continue the chain?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Without next(), the request never reaches later handlers.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should a check that applies only to /jobs routes be mounted?
options: On that router or route, not app-wide
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Scoped mounting avoids running the check for unrelated endpoints.

content.summary: Middleware runs in order and must call next() or respond. Mount each concern at the narrowest scope that fits.

lessons.title: Error Handling in Express
objectives: Use four-argument error middleware
Translate thrown errors into HTTP responses

content.introduction: Express treats any function with four parameters — (err, req, res, next) — as an error handler, and jumps to it as soon as an error occurs.
content.explanation: Calling next(err) anywhere in the chain skips remaining normal middleware and lands in the first error handler, which should log the real error and respond with a generic message so internals never leak to clients. Async handlers need extra care: a rejected promise inside a handler is not automatically routed to Express, so either wrap the handler or let Express 5 handle rejected promises natively. Keep exactly one centralized error handler at the end of the app so every failure produces the same response shape.

examples.title: Centralized error handler
examples.walkthrough: Unknown routes fall through to next(err); the four-argument handler logs the stack but only exposes a safe message to the client.

content.useCase: Turning validation failures, missing records, and unexpected crashes into consistent JSON error responses.

knowledgeCheck.question: How does Express recognize an error-handling middleware?
options: It takes four arguments: err, req, res, next
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The four-parameter signature is what distinguishes it from normal middleware.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should a 500-level response expose to the client?
options: A generic message; details stay in server logs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Internal details can reveal schema, paths, and vulnerabilities.

content.summary: next(err) jumps to the four-argument handler. Log details server-side, return one consistent error shape.

modules.title: Designing REST APIs
modules.description: Model resources, choose methods and status codes correctly, and expose large collections responsibly.
modules.completionCriteria: Design a resource-oriented API with correct verbs, status codes, pagination, and a versioning strategy.

lessons.title: REST Constraints and Resource Design
objectives: Define resources as nouns in the URL
Apply REST constraints to endpoint design

content.introduction: REST models an API as a collection of resources — things with identity — rather than as a set of procedures.
content.explanation: In REST, the URL identifies a resource (a noun) and the HTTP method says what to do with it: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Avoid verbs in paths like /createJob or /getJobById; use GET /jobs and POST /jobs instead. Each resource needs a stable identifier, and the server should be stateless — every request carries the authentication and context it needs. Responses should be self-descriptive (correct status codes and headers) and, where practical, cacheable so intermediaries can reuse them.

examples.title: Procedure-style versus resource-style
examples.walkthrough: The resource style keeps URLs stable nouns and lets the method carry the action, which makes the API predictable from the URL alone.

content.useCase: Public APIs and microservice boundaries where consistency across teams matters more than cleverness.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should a REST URL contain?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The method already carries the action; the path carries identity.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does 'stateless' mean for a REST server?
options: Each request contains all context it needs; no server-side session state
The server keeps user sessions in memory
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Statelessness lets any server instance handle any request.

content.summary: URLs are nouns, methods are verbs, and every request is self-contained. Predictability beats cleverness.

lessons.title: Status Codes, Methods, and Idempotency
objectives: Return accurate status codes
Explain idempotency and when clients retry

content.introduction: Status codes are the API's contract with clients: they decide whether to retry, render an error, or move on.
content.explanation: Group them by class: 2xx success, 4xx the client's mistake, 5xx the server's. Creating a resource returns 201 with a Location header; a successful no-content update returns 204; a missing resource is 404, malformed input 400, failed authentication 401, forbidden 403, and a conflict with existing state 409. Idempotency means performing the same request multiple times has the same effect as once — GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not. That is why clients and gateways may safely retry a timed-out PUT but must be cautious retrying POST unless it carries an idempotency key.

examples.title: Choosing the right status code
examples.walkthrough: Each branch maps to a distinct client action: retry the lookup, fix permissions, resolve the conflict, or treat the POST as created.

content.useCase: Any client that must decide automatically whether a failed request should be retried.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which status code signals that a resource was created?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 201 Created is normally paired with a Location header.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Repeating POST creates duplicate resources unless an idempotency key is used.

content.summary: Use 2xx for success, 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors. Idempotent methods are safe to retry.

lessons.title: Pagination, Filtering, and Versioning
objectives: Paginate collections with a stable strategy
Evolve an API without breaking clients

content.introduction: Collections grow without bound, and APIs change over time — pagination bounds responses, versioning protects clients.
content.explanation: Offset pagination (skip/limit) is simple but shifts rows when data changes mid-read. Cursor-based pagination keys off a stable sort value, so pages stay consistent under inserts — the right default for feeds and large tables. Filtering and sorting belong in the query string: ?status=open&sort=-createdAt. For evolution, additive changes rarely break clients, but removing or renaming fields does; a version segment like /v1/jobs or a version header lets you run both shapes until clients migrate.

examples.title: Cursor pagination endpoint
examples.walkthrough: Fetching one extra row reveals whether more pages exist; the last id becomes the cursor for the next request.

content.useCase: Job boards, activity feeds, and admin lists where results change while users page through them.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main weakness of offset pagination?
options: Rows shift when data is inserted or deleted mid-read
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A changing dataset makes skip/limit skip or repeat items.

knowledgeCheck.question: When do you typically need an API version bump?
options: When a change could break existing clients
When you add a field clients ignore
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Additive, backward-compatible changes do not require a new version.

content.summary: Bound collections with cursor pagination, express filters in the query string, and version only when clients would break.

modules.title: Security, Validation & Testing APIs
modules.description: Protect endpoints, reject bad input early, and prove the API works with automated tests.
modules.completionCriteria: Ship an endpoint that validates input, enforces auth, and passes an automated test suite covering success and failure paths.

lessons.title: Input Validation and Sanitization
objectives: Validate request bodies against a schema
Reject malformed input before it reaches business logic

content.introduction: Every byte a client sends is hostile until proven otherwise — validation is the boundary where bad data dies.
content.explanation: Validate type, shape, and range on every field: strings trimmed and length-limited, numbers bounded, enums checked against allowed values, unknown keys stripped so clients cannot inject fields like role: admin. Validation must run before any database write, and failures should return 400 with a field-by-field message the client can display. Sanitization is a separate step: trim whitespace, normalize casing, and escape values destined for HTML or queries. Validation proves the data is well-formed; it does not replace parameterized queries against injection.

examples.title: Schema validation with Joi
examples.walkthrough: The schema trims titles, bounds numbers, rejects unknown fields like role, and returns 400 before any data is stored.

content.useCase: Registration forms, job postings, and any endpoint that writes client-supplied data.

knowledgeCheck.question: When should request input be validated?
options: At the boundary, before any business logic or database write
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Early rejection keeps untrusted data out of the system entirely.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does .unknown(false) accomplish?
options: It strips or rejects fields not defined in the schema
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Preventing extra keys stops clients from injecting privileged fields.

content.summary: Validate every field at the boundary, reject unknown keys, and return 400 with precise messages.

lessons.title: Authentication, Authorization, and Security Headers
objectives: Distinguish authentication from authorization
Harden responses with headers and safe defaults

content.introduction: Authentication proves who a caller is; authorization decides what that caller may do — conflating them is a common source of privilege bugs.
content.explanation: Typical APIs authenticate with a bearer token (JWT or opaque) sent in the Authorization header, verified by middleware that attaches the identity to the request. Authorization then checks role or ownership per route — a 401 when the token is missing or invalid, a 403 when it is valid but insufficient. Beyond auth, harden every response: set a Content-Type to stop MIME sniffing, add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, a strict Content-Security-Policy, and never echo raw input into HTML. Keep secrets in environment variables, and always use HTTPS so tokens cannot be read in transit.

examples.title: Auth middleware with 401 vs 403
examples.walkthrough: authenticate rejects missing or bad tokens with 401; requireAdmin rejects valid non-admin users with 403 before the handler runs.

content.useCase: Protecting mutating endpoints so only authenticated, appropriately scoped callers can change data.

knowledgeCheck.question: When should an API return 403 instead of 401?
options: The caller is authenticated but lacks permission
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 401 means 'who are you?'; 403 means 'you may not do this'.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should API secrets like signing keys live?
options: In environment variables or a secret manager
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Code and client bundles are readable; secrets there are effectively public.

content.summary: Authenticate with tokens, authorize per route, and harden responses with security headers and env-based secrets.

lessons.title: Testing APIs with Supertest
objectives: Write integration tests against the Express app
Cover success and failure paths

content.introduction: Integration tests send real HTTP requests through your Express app and assert on the responses clients actually receive.
content.explanation: Supertest wraps an HTTP agent around your app object, so you can chain .get/.post, attach .send for the body, and assert on .expect(status) plus body fields — no port or real network needed. Good suites cover the contract: 201 on create, 400 on invalid input, 401 without a token, 404 for a missing id, and 200 on the happy path. Keep tests independent by seeding and cleaning the database per test, and mock only true external boundaries; testing through the real middleware stack catches wiring bugs that unit tests of handlers miss.

examples.title: Integration test for a job endpoint
examples.walkthrough: The first test proves the success contract including the Location header; the second locks in the validation failure so regressions surface immediately.

content.useCase: Continuous integration gates that prevent a bad deploy from breaking API consumers.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does Supertest use to send requests?
options: The exported Express app object, without binding a port
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It performs in-process requests through your real middleware stack.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which cases should an API test suite cover?
options: Success, validation failures, auth failures, and not-found cases
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The contract includes every status code clients rely on.

content.summary: Test through the app with Supertest and assert the full contract: success, validation, auth, and not-found.
